changes.before: In 399 the bishop of Constantinople, the eastern capital, was John, a preacher from Antioch.
changes.reason: Outline: Openings 1 (line 69). Rule: Part 1 opens on one moment in about three sentences; this was a set-up sentence ahead of the moment, and "the eastern capital" is not the outline's wording. The year moves into the fall of Eutropius; the name comes in at the pulpit.

changes.before: Not long before, the emperor's chief eunuch, Eutropius, had a law passed that stripped refugees of the right to shelter in churches.
changes.after: The emperor's chief chamberlain, Eutropius, had a law passed that stripped people who fled into churches of the right to shelter there.
changes.source: The Eutropius law (SS 17337-17341)

changes.before: Then he fell from favor and fled into the cathedral.
changes.after: Soon after, in 399, he fell from favor and himself fled into the cathedral of Constantinople, the emperor's city.
changes.source: his fall and flight, 399 by his consulate (SS 17341-17347, 17360-17364)

changes.before: As he lay trembling under the altar, John climbed into the pulpit and preached against him.
changes.after: As he lay trembling under the altar, the bishop, John Chrysostom, climbed into the pulpit and preached against him.
changes.source: "lay under the table of the altar, mounting the pulpit" (SS 17349-17357)

changes.before: Socrates of Constantinople says some thought John added insult to cruelty.
changes.after: Some thought he was attacking a man already brought low.
changes.source: Socrates: "he seemed to create greater displeasure in some, as he not only denied compassion to the unfortunate, but added insult to cruelty" (SS 17357-17360).

changes.before: John said he spoke to soften the people's hearts toward him, for the church, like a mother, had hidden her enemy under her cloak.
changes.after: John said he spoke to soften the people's hearts, for the church had sheltered its enemy: "When everyone ignored him in his desolation, she alone, like a loving mother, hid him behind her curtains.
changes.source: John: "from a desire to soften your minds towards him, and to induce you to compassion" (N109 17699-17702); "having received her enemy as a captive, she spares him" (N109 17721-17722), offered in answer to those angry that the man "who…

changes.after: She stood against the emperor's anger, the people's fury and unbearable hatred."
changes.source: John: "from a desire to soften your minds towards him, and to induce you to compassion" (N109 17699-17702); "having received her enemy as a captive, she spares him" (N109 17721-17722), offered in answer to those angry that the man "who…

changes.after: His sermons were read for centuries, and the followers who left the church over his fall came back only when his body came home.
changes.source: Socrates: "must read for themselves" (SS 17303-17308); the Augsburg Confession (AUGC 880-881) and Calvin (CALV1 18508-18510) carry the centuries. Socrates VII.45: Proclus "brought back to the Church those who had separated themselves from it on account of Bishop John's deposition…

changes.before: At Antioch John had trained under Diodore, who kept to the literal sense of Scripture.
changes.after: John was born at Antioch, in Syria, and as a priest there for twelve years he preached on what the rich owed the poor.
changes.source: SS 17130-17131 ("a native of Antioch in Syria-Cœle"); PALL 3444-3446 ("For twelve years he was a shining light in the Church of Antioch"); Homily 50 is Antioch's by Homily VII's "our city first crowned itself with the name of Christian"…

changes.after: They decked the altar, where the bread of Communion lies, which Christians call Christ's body, with gold cups and silk.
changes.source: N110 29913-29914: "we offer for this table a gold and jewelled cup". N110 29952-29954: "not forbidding such offerings ... but requiring you, together with them, and before them, to give alms". (first trust read)

changes.before: In a sermon on Matthew, he told his listeners that if they wanted to honor the body of Christ, they must not neglect Him when He is naked.
changes.after: In one sermon he told them to honor Christ in the poor first: "Do you want to honor Christ's body?
changes.source: Q2 against Prevost (N110 29931-29934): "Wouldest thou do honor to Christ's body? Neglect Him not when naked; do not while here thou honorest Him with silken garments, neglect Him perishing without of cold and nakedness." The rendering is faithful. (first…

changes.after: Do not neglect him when he is naked.
changes.source: the sermon on Matthew and Q2, word for word against Prevost (N110 29931-29933; "together with them, and before them, to give alms", 29952-29954)

changes.after: While you honor him here with silk clothes, do not neglect him outside, dying of cold and nakedness."
changes.source: the sermon on Matthew and Q2, word for word against Prevost (N110 29931-29933; "together with them, and before them, to give alms", 29952-29954)

changes.after: He published some of his sermons, and shorthand writers took down others as he spoke.
changes.source: he published some sermons, shorthand writers took others (SS 17304-17306)

changes.after: Both kinds were kept and read.
changes.source: Socrates's "both those which were published by himself, and such as were noted down by short-hand writers ... must read for themselves" (SS 17304-17308).

changes.before: In 398 Eutropius made Theophilus of Alexandria ordain him.
changes.after: In 398 the court chose him as bishop of Constantinople, and Eutropius made Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, ordain him.
changes.source: 398, the court's choice and Eutropius's pressure on Theophilus (SS 17097-17115)

changes.before: Palladius, who wrote John's life and took his side, says he moved the bishop's extravagant spending to the hospital.
changes.after: As bishop he cut the bishop's own spending and gave the money to a hospital.
changes.source: the bishop's spending moved "to the hospital" (PALL 3749-3753)

changes.before: Socrates says his rebukes of men in office turned the tide against him.

changes.after: He corrected his clergy sharply over how they lived and put some of them out of the church, and many came to hate him.
changes.source: Socrates: "more than proper superciliousness, designing to correct the morals of the clergy ... others became his bitter enemies ... expelled many of them from the church" (SS 17262-17275); Sozomen: "ejected some of the clergy" (SS 42798-42800), "hated by the…

changes.before: It is said he was as blunt with the Gothic general Gainas, who asked for a city church for the Arians.
changes.after: When a Gothic general asked for a church inside the city for the Arians, who taught that the Son of God had a beginning, John spoke against it before the emperor.
changes.source: Gainas, the Arians' church, John before the emperor (SS 17368-17372; SS 42887-42894; the gloss, SS 2094-2096)

changes.before: They taught that the Son of God had a beginning.
changes.reason: Outline: Cut first 15 (to the card). Length.

changes.before: Socrates says Theophilus held a grudge, since his favorite had lost the see to John.
changes.after: Socrates, a church historian of the city writing a generation later, says Theophilus also held a grudge, since his own choice for bishop had lost out to John, and that he resolved to unseat him.
changes.source: Socrates's reading of Theophilus, credited (SS 17097, 17375-17381, 17838-17840)

changes.before: Monks Theophilus had driven out of Egypt, in a quarrel over whether God has a human body, came to John for help.
changes.reason: Outline: Cut first 16 (to the card). Length.

changes.before: Socrates says that when Theophilus heard, falsely, that John had given them the Eucharist, he resolved to unseat him.
changes.reason: Outline: Cut first 16 (to the card). Length.

changes.before: He and his bishops, meeting at the Oak near Chalcedon, cited John to appear.
changes.after: Theophilus and his bishops met at a place called the Oak, outside Chalcedon, and summoned John.
changes.source: the Oak and the summons (SS 18275-18283)

changes.after: John refused to come before judges he called his enemies, and asked for a council of the whole church.
changes.source: the refusal and the general council (SS 18285-18291; PHOT 3939-3943)

changes.before: When John refused them as his enemies, they deposed him, Socrates says, for refusing.
changes.after: Socrates says they removed him from office only for refusing to come.
changes.source: "Socrates says ... only for refusing" (SS 18291-18295)

changes.after: A later bishop of Constantinople summed up the meeting's own written record, and they tell it differently: some charges were heard, and then all forty-five bishops voted to remove him.
changes.source: PHOT 3946, 4028-4032, "The first and second counts were then investigated ... forty-five in all ... unanimously". (first trust read)

changes.before: The people rose, and he was recalled.
changes.after: The emperor ordered him into exile, and John gave himself up, but he was soon called back.
changes.source: exile, surrender, recall (SS 18302-18307, 18338-18340)

changes.before: Public games were held at a silver statue of the empress Eudoxia beside the cathedral.
changes.after: Public games were held at a silver statue of the empress Eudoxia, just across the street from the cathedral.
changes.source: SS 18427-18438: "one-half the breadth of the street separated them. At this statue public games were accustomed to be performed".

changes.before: John mocked those who allowed them, and she took this as aimed at her.
changes.after: John mocked those who allowed them, calling the games an insult to the church, and the empress took this as aimed at her and sought another council.
changes.source: "ridiculed those who had enjoined such practices ... another council" (SS 18438-18446)

changes.before: A second council condemned him for taking back his see without a council's leave, and in 404 the emperor sent him into exile.
changes.after: It condemned him for taking back his place as bishop, after his removal, without a council's leave.
changes.source: the second condemnation (SS 18469-18472)

changes.after: Since two councils had condemned him, the emperor barred him from the church, and John was silenced.
changes.source: "two Synods had condemned him ... silenced" (SS 18486-18489)

changes.after: His followers kept Easter in the public baths, and from then on they met apart from the church.
changes.source: Easter in the baths, met apart (SS 18489-18494)

changes.after: In 404 he was taken into exile by force.
changes.source: led into exile by force, 404 by the sixth consulate of Honorius (SS 18496-18502)

changes.after: He was first exiled to Armenia.
changes.source: Cucusus, a city of Armenia (SS 44066-44069)

changes.after: Palladius, who wrote John's life and took his side, says bishops in Syria, seeing the church of Antioch still looking to John, had him moved to Pityus, a more distant place on the Black Sea.
changes.source: PALL 6337-6351: "bishops of Syria ... set to work to get him again transferred elsewhere ... when they saw the Church of Antioch migrating to the Church of Armenia". PALL 6397-6401: "produced a rescript ... John was to be transferred…

changes.before: Palladius says soldiers hurried him toward Pityus, hoping he would die.
changes.after: In his telling, the soldiers hurried John on, saying they had been told his death would bring them promotion.
changes.source: the soldiers' "instructions" and promotion (PALL 6402-6406)

changes.before: He died on the way in 407, with his usual words, "Glory to God for all things."
changes.after: Near Comana he asked for white clothes, took Communion and prayed the words he always used: "Glory to God for all things."
changes.source: white clothes, Communion, "Glory to God for all things" (PALL 6457-6460, 6494-6498; Greek PG47 11682-11683, Δόξα τῷ Θεῷ πάντων ἕνεκεν)

changes.after: He died there, in September 407.
changes.source: September 407 (SS 18609-18612)

changes.before: In 438 Bishop Proclus carried John's body back to Constantinople.
changes.after: In 438 the bishop of Constantinople had the emperor's leave to bring John's body home from Comana.
changes.source: 438, the emperor's leave, the procession, the Apostles, the return (SS 21459-21471)

changes.before: By this, Socrates says, he brought back to the church's communion the followers who had left it over John's deposition.
changes.after: He carried it through the city in procession and laid it in the Church of the Apostles, and those who had left the church over John's fall came back.
changes.source: 438, the emperor's leave, the procession, the Apostles, the return (SS 21459-21471)
